lead: Some liquid mixtures cannot be separated into pure components by ordinary distillation. At an azeotrope the vapour and liquid have the same composition, so the relative volatility is 1 and extra stages achieve nothing. Azeotropic and extractive distillation add a separating agent that changes the vapour-liquid equilibrium and moves the azeotrope or removes it. The agent is an entrainer in azeotropic distillation and a high-boiling solvent in extractive distillation. These methods are used to dehydrate ethanol, purify alcohols and separate close-boiling or azeotrope-forming mixtures.
prereq: You need: 4.1 VLE and relative volatility and 4.4 McCabe-Thiele.

blocks.text: An azeotrope is a composition at which the vapour and liquid in equilibrium have the same mole fractions. For component i, y<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub>. For a pair i and j, relative volatility is α<sub>ij</sub> = (y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub>) ÷ (y<sub>j</sub>/x<sub>j</sub>). At the azeotrope both ratios are equal, so α<sub>ij</sub> = 1. No distillation stage can enrich the vapour beyond this point: the vapour leaving a stage has the same composition as the liquid it came from. A minimum-boiling azeotrope boils lower than both pure components. Ethanol-water is the standard example; at 1 atm it contains about 95.6 mass % ethanol and boils near 78.2 °C. A maximum-boiling azeotrope boils higher than both pure components. On a y-x diagram the equilibrium curve crosses the diagonal at the azeotrope. A water-rich ethanol feed gives water as bottoms and an overhead near the azeotrope. More trays cannot cross the crossing because the driving force is zero.

blocks.where: y<sub>i</sub> and x<sub>i</sub> are mole fractions of i in vapour and liquid; α<sub>ij</sub> is the relative volatility of i to j.

blocks.text: Azeotropic distillation adds an entrainer, a third component that forms a new azeotrope with one or more feed components. The new azeotrope is chosen to leave overhead. It carries one component away while the other leaves at the bottom. The overhead is condensed; if it splits into two liquid layers, a decanter separates the entrainer-rich phase and returns it to the column. The usual scheme has an azeotropic column plus an entrainer-recovery column. The entrainer is recycled, so only small make-up is needed. For ethanol-water, the entrainer forms a low-boiling azeotrope with the component that must be removed overhead — for ethanol dehydration this is normally water, so the overhead is a water-rich entrainer azeotrope that splits in a decanter, and ethanol leaves at the bottom. The entrainer must be selective, form an azeotrope that is easy to break, be thermally stable, and be safe and cheap. It leaves with the overhead, unlike an extractive solvent.

Extractive distillation feeds a high-boiling, relatively nonvolatile solvent near the top of the column. The solvent does not form a new azeotrope in the usual case. It changes the activity coefficients of the feed components, so their relative volatility changes. One component becomes more volatile and leaves overhead; the other travels down with the solvent. The bottom product is solvent plus the less volatile component. A second column strips or distils the solvent from that mixture. The lean solvent is cooled and recycled to the top of the extractive column. For ethanol-water, a high-boiling solvent such as ethylene glycol makes ethanol the overhead product and sends water down with the solvent.

items: Feed enters below the top of the extractive column.
Solvent enters above the feed and flows down the column.
The more volatile product leaves overhead.
The bottoms, solvent plus the less volatile component, goes to solvent recovery.
Recovered solvent returns to the top of the extractive column.

blocks.text: Pressure-swing distillation uses two columns at different pressures. The azeotrope composition shifts with pressure, so the overhead from one column can be fed to a second column where it is no longer at the azeotrope. No added solvent is needed, but the pressure change costs energy and capital. It works only when the shift is large enough. Choose azeotropic distillation when a suitable entrainer is available and a new azeotrope can be broken easily. Choose extractive distillation when a selective high-boiling solvent is available and the solvent can be recovered simply. In both cases the agent changes equilibrium; it does not violate it. The agent is recycled, so solvent losses and energy for recovery set the operating cost.

figure.caption: Extractive distillation: feed enters the extractive column, ethanol-rich overhead leaves, and the high-boiling solvent is recovered and recycled to the top.

spec.aria: Extractive distillation block diagram: feed enters the extractive column, overhead product leaves, solvent is recovered and recycled.

examples.question: An ethanol-water feed of 100 kg contains 50 mass % ethanol. At 1 atm the minimum-boiling azeotrope is about 95.6 mass % ethanol. Ordinary distillation from this water-rich feed can give pure water as bottoms and an overhead at the azeotrope. Find the maximum overhead mass if the overhead is at 95.6 mass % ethanol and the ethanol is taken overhead.
steps: Basis: feed F = 100 kg and ethanol mass fraction in feed x<sub>F</sub> = 0.50.
The overhead is at the azeotrope: x<sub>D</sub> = 0.956 ethanol mass fraction.
Ethanol balance with all ethanol taken overhead: D × 0.956 = 50 kg.
Total balance: B = F − D = 100 − 52.301 = 47.699 kg.
Bottoms are essentially water. Rounded: D = 52.3 kg and B = 47.7 kg.
Ethanol above 95.6 mass % cannot be obtained by ordinary distillation; use azeotropic or extractive distillation.
examples.answer: The maximum overhead is about 52.3 kg at 95.6 mass % ethanol, and the bottoms is about 47.7 kg, essentially water.
examples.check:
ethanol_in_feed = 0.50 * 100
azeotrope = 0.956
D = ethanol_in_feed / azeotrope
B = 100 - D
print(round(D, 1))
print(round(B, 1))

traps: A longer column can cross an azeotrope. At α = 1 the stages do nothing; the equilibrium curve meets the diagonal.
Entrainer and extractive solvent both leave at the bottom. The entrainer forms a new azeotrope and leaves overhead; the extractive solvent leaves at the bottom and is recycled.
The azeotrope composition is the same at every pressure. It shifts with pressure, which is the basis of pressure-swing distillation.
Mass % and mole % are interchangeable in the ethanol-water azeotrope value. 95.6 mass % ethanol is not 95.6 mol % ethanol.
Any added liquid will break the azeotrope. The agent must change relative volatility and must be recoverable economically.

quiz.q: Define an azeotrope in terms of y<sub>i</sub> and x<sub>i</sub>.
quiz.a: An azeotrope is a composition where the vapour and liquid in equilibrium have the same mole fractions, so y<sub>i</sub> = x<sub>i</sub> and the relative volatility α = 1.

quiz.q: Why does adding more theoretical stages not move an overhead past a minimum-boiling azeotrope?
quiz.a: At the azeotrope the vapour and liquid compositions are equal. The driving force for separation is zero and α = 1, so extra stages cannot enrich the vapour further.

quiz.q: A feed of 100 kg contains 40 mass % ethanol in water. Ordinary distillation gives an overhead at 95.6 mass % ethanol and takes all ethanol overhead. Find the overhead mass.
quiz.a: Ethanol in feed = 0.40 × 100 = 40 kg. D = 40 ÷ 0.956 = 41.84 kg. Rounded, D = 41.8 kg.

quiz.q: Compare where the entrainer and the extractive solvent leave the distillation scheme, and why.
quiz.a: An entrainer forms a new azeotrope and leaves with the overhead product; it is separated later and recycled. An extractive solvent is high-boiling, leaves at the bottom with the less volatile component, and is recovered in a second column and recycled to the top.

quiz.q: Why is the extractive solvent fed near the top of the column?
quiz.a: Feeding near the top keeps a high solvent concentration throughout the column. The solvent changes activity coefficients and relative volatility along the stages.

quiz.q: For a mixture, y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub> = 1.2 and y<sub>j</sub>/x<sub>j</sub> = 1.2. Find α<sub>ij</sub>. (Because the two ratios are equal, α<sub>ij</sub> = 1, the azeotropic condition.)
quiz.a: α<sub>ij</sub> = (y<sub>i</sub>/x<sub>i</sub>) ÷ (y<sub>j</sub>/x<sub>j</sub>) = 1.2 ÷ 1.2 = 1. Equal ratios mean the mixture is at an azeotrope.

quiz.q: When is pressure-swing distillation preferred over extractive distillation?
quiz.a: Pressure-swing is preferred when the azeotrope composition shifts enough with pressure and no added solvent is wanted. Extractive distillation is preferred when a selective high-boiling solvent is available and easy to recover.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industrial ethanol dehydration often uses extractive distillation with a high-boiling solvent, or azeotropic distillation with a light entrainer, and both are combined with heat integration. Newer work screens ionic liquids and deep eutectic solvents as nonvolatile extractive agents, and divided-wall columns for energy saving. Search for "ethanol dehydration extractive distillation solvent screening" and "pressure-swing distillation azeotrope".
